aapl-record-rally.headline: Apple hits record high as July rally nears best month in four years
aapl-record-rally.body_md:
Apple shares touched a fresh record on Thursday, rising 1.8% to extend a July run that has now reached 15.2% for the month — the stock's best monthly showing in roughly four years. Within the Magnificent Seven, only one member has outrun it this month; Apple sits second, and it has done so while the Nasdaq-100 (QQQ) has actually shed close to 5% in July as semiconductor names sold off.

That divergence is the actual news here. Apple has spent much of the past two years as the group's laggard on AI narrative grounds — no chip franchise, no cloud arm generating the kind of capex headlines that moved Nvidia or Microsoft. This month the rotation has run the other way, with investors funneling into a company whose AI story is still, largely, a promise.

HSBC gave that rotation a fresh nudge Thursday, upgrading Apple to "Buy" from "Hold" and setting a $366 price target — about 10% above Thursday's close. The bank's move stands out against the broader analyst field: of 47 analysts covering the stock, 28 rate it Buy or higher, 16 sit at Hold, and three are at Sell or below, with an average price target of $315.79, more than 5% under current levels. HSBC, in other words, is more bullish than the Street's center of gravity, not confirming it.

## What's actually driving it

The fundamentals underpinning the rally are thin. Apple has pushed through price increases on MacBooks, iPads, HomePods and Apple TV hardware, alongside a modest AppleCare+ subscription bump, and there is speculation the next iPhone cycle carries higher price tags too — pricing power rather than volume growth. Reports that Apple is exploring an AI chip acquisition have added a speculative kicker. And the company's leadership handover is now on the calendar: Tim Cook moves to executive chairman on September 1, handing the CEO role to hardware chief John Ternus after 25 years at the company, most recently overseeing the Apple Silicon transition.

None of that is a catalyst in the earnings sense — there's no print, no guidance raise, no product launch driving the move. What's visible is money moving within the Mag Seven cohort as AI-capex anxiety weighs on the more chip-exposed names, and Apple, insulated from that specific worry, catching the flow.

The next real test arrives with Apple's fiscal third-quarter earnings, expected in late July, when the market will find out whether the pricing moves are showing up in margin — or whether the rally has been running ahead of the numbers.

siemens-energy-rebrand.headline: Siemens Energy to rebrand as Omterra, dropping parent's name
siemens-energy-rebrand.body_md:
Siemens Energy told the market on July 14 that it is preparing to stop being Siemens Energy. The Munich-based turbine and grid equipment maker — spun out of Siemens AG in 2020 — said it will retire the Siemens name entirely and unite itself and its wind-power arm, Siemens Gamesa, under a single new brand: Omterra. The rollout begins later this year and will run in stages over roughly 18 months.

The headline reason is contractual, not existential. When Siemens AG carved out its energy business six years ago, it granted the new company a time-limited license to keep using the Siemens name — a licensing fee structured as a percentage of revenue, running to roughly €300 million in the most recent year, under a deal that extends to 2030. CEO Christian Bruch put the logic plainly: "Since our spin-off, it has been clear that the licensed Siemens Energy brand would be available to us for a limited period," he said, adding that the company is now "strategically, operationally, and financially positioned" to go it alone. Shedding the license years ahead of its 2030 expiry removes a nine-figure annual cost from the books.

## What's actually changing

Operationally, not much — yet. Siemens Energy says existing contracts stay valid without new signatures, and equipment nameplates won't change in the near term. But vendors and partners will need to re-register the new corporate name in procurement systems, and the bigger structural move is consolidation: Siemens Gamesa, the loss-prone wind turbine unit that has weighed on group earnings for years, gets folded into the same brand umbrella as the profitable gas-turbine and grid-technology business. Whether that reflects closer operational integration or simply tidier marketing is not yet clear from the announcement.

![Siemens Energy logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f2/Siemens_Energy_logo.svg)

## Reading it as a market signal

Rebrands of this scale invite scrutiny beyond the marketing brief, and the timing is notable: it lands as demand for grid and turbine equipment is running hot. A US heatwave this month pushed the PJM grid interconnection — spanning Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Maryland — to a record peak load of 166 gigawatts, intensifying the data-center-driven demand for exactly the equipment Siemens Energy sells. Shares rose 3.5% to €153.92 on announcement day, part of a run that has the stock up roughly 66% year-to-date, though still 21% below its April high of €195.54.

Analysts remain split on what the stock is worth even after the brand news. Jefferies held a "Buy" rating with a €215 target; JPMorgan's target sits at €235. Barclays, by contrast, downgraded the stock to "Underweight" on July 7 while nudging its own target up to €130 — a spread of roughly €105 between the most bullish and bearest calls, underscoring that the disagreement is about earnings durability, not the rebrand itself.

## What it isn't — for now

Siemens Energy has been explicit that Omterra is a brand transition, not a change in strategy, ownership structure, or business mix. There is no announced spinoff, no divestiture of Gamesa, no new capital structure. Still, a company doesn't drop a parent's name — one still recognized in more than 90 countries — without inviting the question of how independent it intends to become. The Siemens AG stake in the business, and the terms of any residual relationship after 2030, will matter more to that question than the logo does.

The practical test comes over the next 18 months, as the name changes on offices, contracts and eventually hardware. The nearer one is Siemens Energy's next earnings report, when investors will get a fuller picture of how much of that €300 million in freed-up licensing cost flows straight to margin — and whether Gamesa's integration under one brand comes with any integration of its numbers.

boeing-737-max-approval.headline: Boeing nears FAA approval that could unlock delayed 737 Max deliveries
boeing-737-max-approval.body_md:
Boeing is within weeks — possibly days — of clearing the last regulatory hurdle standing between it and a fleet of finished, unsold jets parked on the tarmac in Moses Lake, Washington.

The Federal Aviation Administration is nearing certification of the 737 MAX 7, the smallest and longest-delayed variant of Boeing's best-selling family, according to reporting from the Wall Street Journal and multiple aviation trade outlets this week. Boeing's own program manager for 737 derivatives has said the company is "95% complete with all our certification deliverables" on the MAX 7. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has said he has identified no issues that would block sign-off before the end of the year, and industry trackers now put MAX 7 approval as likely by the end of July — thirteen years after Southwest Airlines launched the program.

![A Southwest Airlines Boeing 737 MAX on approach](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/N8707P_Southwest_Boeing_737_MAX-8.jpg)

**In one sentence:** The FAA is close to certifying Boeing's 737 MAX 7, which could free roughly 30 finished jets sitting idle and unlock deliveries stalled since 2021.

## What's actually being signed off

The holdup was never about volume production — it was a single component. In 2021, Boeing engineers found that the engine anti-ice system on the MAX 7 and MAX 10, if left running too long by pilots after icing conditions passed, could overheat the composite nacelle inlet enough to crack it and shed debris in flight. Regulators let the already-certified MAX 8, 8-200 and 9 keep flying, but held the line on the two newer variants until Boeing redesigned the part. That redesign work — which Boeing says also cuts noise and vibration — has now moved through flight testing: the MAX 10 has completed roughly 98% of its certification test program and entered the FAA's final inspection phase.

Separately, the FAA is weighing whether to restore Boeing's authority to issue its own airworthiness certificates on new 737s — delegated sign-off power it stripped after the two fatal MAX crashes in 2018 and 2019. Getting that authority back would speed up every delivery going forward, not just the MAX 7 and MAX 10.

## The backlog waiting to move

About 30 finished MAX 7 airframes are already sitting at Moses Lake, built and waiting for a signature. Southwest holds roughly 90% of all MAX 7 orders — 289 aircraft — and has used the wait to keep older 737-700s in service longer than planned. Around nine completed MAX 10s are similarly parked; that variant alone makes up more than a quarter of Boeing's remaining 737 MAX backlog, with United (277 jets), Alaska Airlines (105) and others on the order book. Combined MAX 7 and MAX 10 orders top 1,700 aircraft.

Even with certification, deliveries won't be instant. Southwest's own 2025 annual report projected zero MAX 7 deliveries this year, pushing first handoffs into early 2027 as the aircraft moves through production ramp-up and customer acceptance. The MAX 10 is expected to trail further behind, with Bedford pointing to certification before year-end rather than a specific delivery date.

## A muted market response

Boeing shares have not moved much on the certification news itself — up roughly half a percent after hours when the story first broke, then essentially flat to lower the following session, and down over 3% on July 13 amid separate reports of supply-chain strain on the MAX production ramp. The tepid reaction reflects a stock that has spent years pricing in certification as eventual rather than urgent; the harder question for investors is less "will the FAA sign off" and more whether Boeing's supply chain can turn a certification into a delivery cadence.

The next concrete marker is the MAX 7 certification decision itself, expected by month's end. After that, attention shifts to the MAX 10, which Bedford has pegged for approval before the close of 2026, and to Boeing's next earnings call for an update on how quickly the Moses Lake backlog actually starts moving to customers.

fed-officials-inflation-outlook.headline: Fed officials split on inflation risk as AI capex and tariffs cloud outlook
fed-officials-inflation-outlook.body_md:
Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan spent Thursday doing something unusual for a central banker: making the dovish case and the hawkish case in the same breath. Wages, she told an audience in Houston, are not currently feeding inflation. But she is worried they could start. And by the end of her remarks, she had become the first Fed official to publicly call for another interest-rate increase since Kevin Warsh took over as chair in May.

That combination — currently-benign, structurally-worried — captures where the Fed finds itself two weeks before its July 28-29 meeting. Logan's Kansas City counterpart, Jeff Schmid, spent the same day arguing the opposite framing is dangerous: don't assume anything about this inflation is temporary. Between them, traders got a clearer picture of the Fed's internal debate and no clearer picture of what it will do next.

## Wages now, AI later

Logan's headline line was reassurance: current wage growth, in her assessment, is not providing inflationary pressure relative to productivity. But she qualified it immediately, noting that some Texas businesses have told her they are raising pay faster than expected, and calling a wage-price spiral an "early days" risk rather than a live one.

Where she was more definitive was on artificial intelligence. Investment demand tied to AI, she said, is "big, real" and carries near-term inflationary effects — even as she remains "very optimistic" about the technology's long-run productivity payoff. She extended the point to the physical infrastructure behind it: electricity prices driven by data-center demand will likely be, in her words, "another source of modest inflationary pressure," a conclusion she said holds even under the most conservative estimates. US data-center electricity consumption is projected to more than double by 2030, and Logan's remarks put a Fed governor's name behind treating that buildout as a genuine price-pressure channel, not a rounding error.

![Data center server infrastructure of the kind driving new electricity demand](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/86/Global_Switch_Data_Centre.jpg)

On energy more broadly, Logan pointed to a supply-side wrinkle that complicates the usual story about high prices calling forth new output: gas takeaway capacity and other midstream infrastructure constraints are limiting how much producers can actually ramp up even with oil prices elevated, she said, and recent gains in US oil exports have come mostly from drawing down inventories rather than new production. With fighting in the Middle East now in its fifth night and the US Navy moving to disable a non-compliant tanker near the Strait of Hormuz, that supply bottleneck is not an abstraction — it's a mechanism by which a geopolitical shock could show up in pump prices faster than domestic producers can respond.

## The rate call

All of that fed into the sharper news of the day: Logan, a voting FOMC member this year, said "modestly" higher interest rates would better balance the outlook and risks, arguing inflation "has been too high, for too long" and that labor, spending and financial data don't show current policy meaningfully restraining the economy. Her framing was explicitly asymmetric — "better modest restriction now than severe restriction later" — the same logic she has used since calling for a rate increase back in early June. Consumer prices were running 3.5% above a year earlier as of the latest reading, with wholesale costs up 5.5%; Logan has said her best guess is that inflation is heading toward the "mid-2s," not all the way back to the Fed's 2% target on its own.

Schmid, speaking at a Kansas City Fed forum in Nebraska, arrived at a similar policy conclusion from a different angle. He called the labor market "roughly stable" — in balance, with growth showing resilience — but said inflation is "proving persistent across a broad selection of goods and services" and is "concerning." More pointedly, he rejected the idea that the Fed should "look through" particular categories of price increases, the framing that treated 2021's inflation as transitory: "I am uncomfortable ever assuming that a burst of inflation is likely to be temporary," he said, adding that inflation shocks are "not intrinsically transitory." He also tied the Fed's credibility to process, arguing that accountability requires the institution to explain how it makes decisions and to tolerate open criticism of them.

![Kevin Warsh, who became Federal Reserve Chair in May 2026](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/30/Kevin_Warsh%2C_Federal_Reserve_photo_portrait.jpg)

## Balance sheet, and a nod to continuity

Logan used part of her remarks to reframe a longer-running debate over the Fed's balance sheet, arguing the goal should be an efficient and effective balance sheet rather than a target for its size — and floating, without specifics, that a more optimal regulatory liquidity regime for banks could eventually allow the balance sheet to shrink further. Neither point came with a timeline or proposal attached; both read as an invitation to a future debate rather than a policy shift underway now.

She closed on institutional footing, saying Fed meetings and the data-driven structure of policymaking "have not changed a bit" under Warsh, and that the new chair — who took the gavel from Jerome Powell in May — shares "tremendous dedication to the institution" that Powell showed. It was a notable thing to say out loud, at a moment when Warsh has already announced task forces to overhaul major Fed operations: Logan was vouching for continuity precisely because continuity is the question markets are asking about a new chair. She also flagged a more local concern — that immigration restrictions are squeezing the Texas labor force, even as the resulting slower population growth has made otherwise-modest payroll gains look consistent with a balanced labor market rather than a weakening one.

## What it adds up to

Strip away the specific topics and the throughline is this: two regional Fed presidents, one dovish-sounding on current conditions and one hawkish-sounding on principle, reached the same place — modestly tighter policy is warranted, and none of the AI investment boom, data-center power demand or oil-supply constraints currently in view point toward inflation cooling on its own. That both arrived there from different starting premises is precisely what leaves traders without a clean signal: it looks less like a Fed converging on a model of the economy and more like several officials independently concluding that the risks skew the same direction for different reasons. Logan is a voter this year; Schmid is not. The next hard data point is the July 28-29 FOMC meeting, where the question is no longer whether officials are worried about inflation stickiness, but whether Logan's rate-hike call — the first under Warsh — finds company at the table.

iran-hormuz-tanker-disabled.headline: US Navy disables non-compliant tanker as Iran strikes enter fifth night
iran-hormuz-tanker-disabled.body_md:
Just after 2 p.m. Eastern on Thursday, American warplanes began a fifth consecutive night of strikes on Iran. By the time the last aircraft turned for home near dawn Friday, CENTCOM said it had hit targets spread from the southwest coast to the Pakistani border. A few hours earlier and a few hundred miles to the south, Marines from the 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit had fast-roped onto the deck of a crude tanker in the Gulf of Oman — the clearest signal yet that the United States is no longer content to police the Strait of Hormuz from a distance.

The two threads are the same story. Washington's air campaign against Iran, now well into its fifth month since strikes began on February 28, has entered a phase focused less on symbolic deterrence and more on physically controlling the chokepoint through which roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil passes.

![U.S. Navy sailors conduct a visit, board, search and seizure boarding exercise from a rigid-hull inflatable boat.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/20/Visit_board_search_and_seizure_VBSS_team.jpg)

## Bridges down at Bandar Khamir

The night's strikes reached further inland than usual. Iran's semi-official Fars news agency reported that a bridge in Bandar Khamir, a coastal district of Hormozgan province, was hit; other Iranian outlets, including Tasnim, said as many as three bridges were struck in the same area, among them the main highway link between the port city of Bandar Abbas and Lar in neighbouring Fars province. Iranian media said the strikes landed while civilian traffic was crossing, with vehicles thrown from the roadway; Fars put the toll at seven dead and nine wounded, figures that have not been independently verified. Power was knocked out across parts of the surrounding Kahurestan area and mobile networks went down.

The targeting pattern is not incidental. Bandar Abbas is Iran's principal port and the closest major population and logistics center to the strait itself. Cutting the bridges, together with reported strikes on an airport, a railway line and a communications tower in the same stretch of coast, reads as an effort to sever the port from Iran's interior — road and rail arteries rather than military hardware. CENTCOM has not detailed individual targets beyond saying the goal is to "further degrade Iranian military capabilities," and has offered no damage assessment of its own.

## The blockade tightens

The more novel development sits offshore. Trump reinstated the naval blockade of Iranian ports on July 14 after a mid-summer lull, and CENTCOM has been posting a running tally of enforcement since. As of Thursday, the command said it had redirected three commercial vessels attempting to reach Iranian ports, disabled one that refused to comply, and boarded a fifth to confirm it was operating within the rules. The disabled vessel was the Belma, an empty Curaçao-flagged tanker that U.S. forces struck with Hellfire missiles on its smokestack after it pressed on toward Kharg Island — Iran's main crude export terminal — despite warnings.

The boarding was more theatrical: CENTCOM released footage of armed Marines from the Camp Pendleton-based 11th MEU, deployed aboard the amphibious assault ship USS Boxer, fast-roping from helicopters onto the deck of the M/T Wen Yao, a previously sanctioned crude carrier, to conduct what the command called a "verification boarding." In its own words, CENTCOM described the strait as "free and open," with the caveat that applies to every vessel except those trying to breach what it called America's "steel wall" around Iranian ports. That framing — open to the world, closed to Iran — is a narrower blockade than the version Trump floated a week earlier, when he briefly threatened a 20% fee on all cargo transiting the strait before walking it back under pressure from shippers and Gulf allies.

![An MH-60S Sea Hawk helicopter approaches the flight deck of USS Boxer during a replenishment at sea.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/19/160329-N-GZ228-091_160329-N-GZ228-091.jpg)

## What it's doing to the water

The numbers underneath the enforcement statistics are the real story for anyone hedging energy exposure. Traffic through the strait has thinned sharply: roughly 18 to 22 vessels a day before the current round of fighting resumed, versus as few as six in a twelve-hour window earlier this month. Shipping brokers estimate close to 230 loaded tankers are effectively stranded inside the Gulf with no port willing to receive them. War-risk insurance premiums, which cover vessels operating in the zone, have climbed to four or five times pre-war levels since fighting first broke out in February — a cost that compounds every time a tanker owner has to reroute or wait out a boarding.

Brent crude has responded accordingly, trading near $85 a barrel this week, close to a one-month high and reversing roughly a third of the price decline that followed the interim peace deal reached after the February war's opening phase, when an Israeli strike killed Iran's supreme leader and touched off the broader conflict. Analysts tracking the campaign have floated $100 a barrel as the next threshold if the current intensity — nightly strikes plus active interdiction — holds for several more weeks. None of that requires the strait to actually close; it only requires insurers, shipowners and traders to keep pricing in the chance that it might.

## What comes next

The blockade's own history is a caution against assuming this is the peak. During its first run this spring, before a short-lived truce, CENTCOM said it redirected more than 140 vessels and disabled nine over roughly two months — figures far above where the current, five-day-old restart stands. If enforcement scales the way it did then, boardings like the Wen Yao's are likely to become routine rather than newsworthy. The nearer-term variables to watch are whether Thursday's bridge strikes near Bandar Abbas mark a shift toward hitting logistics infrastructure rather than military sites, and whether Tehran responds to the port city's isolation with retaliation at sea, where its Revolutionary Guard has previously laid mines and harassed shipping. The next CENTCOM enforcement update and the next OPEC-adjacent commentary on Brent's trajectory are the two data points most likely to move first.

airbus-a330neo-orders.headline: Airbus eyes fresh A330neo orders after $10bn SAS deal
airbus-a330neo-orders.body_md:
Airbus is trying to turn one big order into a pattern. Two weeks after Scandinavian carrier SAS signed for up to 40 A330 family widebodies in a deal worth more than $10 billion, the planemaker is in advanced talks with Saudi budget carrier flynas and Germany's Condor over further A330neo purchases — agreements that people familiar with the discussions say could be signed as early as next week's Farnborough International Airshow.

![Airbus A330neo, showing the type's distinctive curved wingtip sharklets](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/94/Airbus_A330neo%2C_new_sharklets.jpg)

**In one sentence:** Airbus is closing in on fresh A330neo orders from flynas and Condor that could be signed at Farnborough, building on SAS's $10 billion deal.

## The SAS deal as backdrop

SAS's order, signed in Copenhagen on June 30 between chief executive Anko van der Werff and Airbus commercial sales chief Benoît de Saint-Exupéry, is the largest aircraft purchase in the carrier's 80-year history. It covers new A330-900neo jets alongside additional A330-300s, with list-price value above $10 billion and firm orders reported at 18 aircraft within the wider 40-jet program. The A330-900neo, powered by Rolls-Royce Trent 7000 engines, seats 287 to 303 passengers in three-class configuration and burns roughly 25% less fuel per seat than the aircraft it replaces — the pitch Airbus has used to sell the type since it entered service in 2018.

## Flynas and Condor talks

Bloomberg and Reuters reported this week that flynas, the Saudi low-cost carrier expanding under the kingdom's Vision 2030 tourism push, is close to firming up eight more A330neos, which would take its total order book to roughly 30 of the type with first deliveries expected in 2027. Condor, the German leisure carrier, is separately discussing six aircraft that would extend a fleet already built around the A330neo to around two dozen jets — though industry sources have cautioned that the Condor talks are less advanced than flynas's and could still fall through before Farnborough opens.

Airbus's commercial aircraft chief, Christian Scherer, framed the flynas discussions in terms of commonality rather than raw growth: "The A330neo will allow flynas to further grow into widebody markets by building on the A320, benefiting from Airbus' unique commonality." That logic — narrow-body operators graduating to widebodies within the same parts and training ecosystem — is the same case Airbus has made to SAS and to Middle Eastern carriers building out long-haul networks.

## What a cluster of orders would signal

No single order settles an argument about aircraft demand, but three widebody deals inside a month is a different signal than one. It would suggest airlines are still willing to commit billions to long-haul capacity even as macro conditions — tariff uncertainty, mixed signals on inflation, and jittery capital markets — have made other corporate spending more cautious. It also keeps pressure on Boeing, whose competing 787 program is contending with its own production and certification questions, to defend its widebody backlog at the same airshow.

For Rolls-Royce, the sole engine supplier on the A330neo via its Trent 7000, each additional order is effectively locked-in aftermarket revenue for decades of servicing. For Airbus, the more immediate value is momentum: a Farnborough news cycle stacked with widebody signings reinforces the sense that the A330neo, a jet some analysts once dismissed as a stopgap ahead of a re-engined successor, still has commercial legs.

None of the flynas or Condor terms are finalized, and neither airline has confirmed aircraft counts publicly. The Farnborough Airshow opens next week, and that is the first point at which any of this converts from reported talks into signed paper.

asml-price-target-raise.headline: JPMorgan lifts ASML price target to $2,400, keeps overweight
asml-price-target-raise.body_md:
JPMorgan raised its price target on ASML Holding to $2,400 from $2,200 on Friday, maintaining its overweight rating on the Dutch chip-equipment maker two days after the company posted second-quarter results that beat estimates and lifted its full-year outlook for the second time in 2026.

The target implies roughly 34% upside from ASML's Friday price of around $1,790, where shares slipped about 1.4% even as the bank turned more bullish. It is JPMorgan's second target increase on the stock since June, when it raised the figure to $2,200 from $1,813.

**In one sentence:** JPMorgan raised its ASML price target to $2,400 from $2,200 and kept its overweight rating after the chip-equipment maker's Q2 beat and raised 2026 guidance.

![ASML headquarters in Veldhoven, the Netherlands](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ae/ASML_headquarters_Veldhoven.jpg)

## The numbers behind the call

ASML reported €9.3 billion in net sales and €2.9 billion in net income for the second quarter, released Monday. The company raised its full-year 2026 sales guidance to a range of €43 billion to €45 billion, up from the €36 billion to €40 billion range it had set in April — the second upward revision this year. Gross margin guidance for the year now sits between 54% and 56%, and the company pointed investors to a stronger third quarter still, forecasting €11 billion to €12 billion in net sales with margins of 55% to 57%.

Chief executive Christophe Fouquet described order intake through the first half of the year as "extremely strong," attributing the pace to customers accelerating capacity plans tied to AI-related chip production. ASML said it is now largely booked for 2027 and plans to expand capacity by 30% in each of the next two years across both its extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and deep ultraviolet immersion tool lines, with EUV order books already extending into 2028.

## Why the stock dipped anyway

Despite the beat, ASML shares fell on the day of the report — a reminder that in a stock that has more than doubled over the past year, a strong quarter is not automatically a rally trigger when expectations have already priced in most of the good news. ASML remains roughly 11% below its 52-week high near $2,000, even after the run.

That gap between operational performance and share reaction is the backdrop for JPMorgan's move. The bank's target bump is less a fresh insight than a mechanical response to the guidance raise — the kind of routine analyst housekeeping that follows almost every earnings beat from a company this closely tracked. It carries no new rating change, no revised thesis, and no departure from the overweight stance JPMorgan has held through ASML's price target climbing from $1,813 to $2,200 to $2,400 across three revisions this year alone.

## The chokepoint argument

What gives the note weight beyond routine coverage maintenance is ASML's position in the chip supply chain. The company is the sole global supplier of the EUV lithography systems needed to print the most advanced logic and memory chips — machines that run to roughly €150 million apiece, weigh around 150 tonnes, and ship in some 250 crates. No competitor makes an equivalent tool, which gives ASML unusual pricing power and visibility into demand trends across the entire AI infrastructure buildout, from Nvidia's GPU suppliers to memory makers like SK Hynix and Samsung.

That chokepoint status is why ASML's order commentary tends to move sentiment across the broader chip-equipment and foundry complex, even when the news itself — a target bump, a maintained rating — is unremarkable on its own terms.

## What's next

ASML's next scheduled update is its third-quarter report, expected in October, which will show whether the €11 billion to €12 billion sales guidance holds and whether 2027 order books — which the company says are already largely full — continue to build. Until then, JPMorgan's $2,400 target functions mostly as a marker of how far Wall Street now expects the AI-driven capex cycle to run, rather than a signal of anything new.

jera-us-listing-study.headline: Japan's JERA studies US listing as it expands overseas
jera-us-listing-study.body_md:
JERA, the Japanese utility that generates roughly three in ten kilowatt-hours consumed in the country, has begun studying a listing on a US stock exchange, according to people familiar with the matter cited in a Reuters exclusive. No decision has been made on timing, venue or size, the sources said — but the study itself marks a shift for a company that has spent a decade absorbing the fallout of Fukushima rather than courting Wall Street.

JERA was created in 2015 as a 50-50 merger of the fuel and thermal-power units of Tokyo Electric Power Company and Chubu Electric Power, a consolidation forced partly by the need to rebuild TEPCO's balance sheet after the 2011 nuclear disaster. The resulting company inherited nearly 40% of Japan's thermal generation capacity and became one of the world's largest buyers and traders of liquefied natural gas, moving around 35 million tonnes a year.

## A widening American footprint

A US listing would formalize a pivot that has been building in plain sight. JERA agreed in September to pay roughly $1.7 billion for Haynesville shale gas assets from a Blackstone-and-Williams-backed venture — its first move into US gas production — and separately signed a letter of intent for supply from Alaska's $44 billion LNG export project. In June, Nikkei reported the company would spend about ¥500 billion ($3 billion) building a gas-fired power plant to feed a US data center directly, sidestepping grid bottlenecks tied to America's AI-driven power crunch. Offshore, JERA folded its wind business into JERA Nex bp, a London-headquartered joint venture with BP formed last August with a 13-gigawatt project pipeline spanning the US, Europe and Asia-Pacific.

## The capital question

The listing study also answers a question JERA has been dodging since April 2024, when it first told Bloomberg it might tap outside investors — "trillions of yen" would be needed, it said then — to fund a 2035 strategy built around ¥5 trillion in investment, a sixfold expansion of renewables capacity to 20 gigawatts, and targets of ¥350 billion in net profit and ¥700 billion in EBITDA. A US listing would let JERA raise dollar-denominated capital closer to where much of that spending — shale gas, LNG terminals, gas-fired plants for data centers — is now happening, rather than relying solely on Tokyo markets or its two utility parents.

Whether JERA follows through will say something about how far Japan's post-Fukushima utility consolidation can travel. A company assembled to stabilize two regional monopolies is now weighing whether its next chapter gets financed in New York. Watch for confirmation of an underwriter mandate or bourse choice — the next concrete marker in a process JERA's sources say remains at an early, exploratory stage.

quantinuum-rolls-royce-deal.headline: Quantinuum strikes industrial-design deal with Rolls-Royce
quantinuum-rolls-royce-deal.body_md:
Rolls-Royce builds jet engines that have to survive forces most materials shouldn't. Getting the physics right before metal is cut requires simulating how air and combustion gases move through a turbine — fluid dynamics calculations so demanding that even modern supercomputers strain under the detail engineers want. That bottleneck is the reason Rolls-Royce just signed up for a multi-year collaboration with Quantinuum, the quantum computing company that went public on Nasdaq in June, to see whether quantum hardware can help.

The agreement, announced July 14, also brings in Riverlane, a Cambridge-based quantum error-correction specialist, and EPCC, the University of Edinburgh's supercomputing centre. The plan is narrow and specific: test hybrid quantum-classical workflows on real gas turbine fluid dynamics problems, using Quantinuum's Helios machine — a 98-qubit trapped-ion system the company markets as the most accurate commercial quantum computer available — alongside conventional supercomputers.

![A Rolls-Royce Trent turbofan engine, the kind of hardware whose airflow modeling the quantum partnership targets](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fe/Rolls-Royce_Trent_1000_jet_engine.jpg)

## What's actually being tested

Rolls-Royce Fellow Leigh Lapworth described the work as building on five years of prior algorithm development between Rolls-Royce, Riverlane and EPCC — this agreement moves that work onto Quantinuum's hardware. Quantinuum CEO Rajeeb Hazra framed the appeal in blunt terms: "The computing demands of simulating complex fluid dynamics are a major challenge," he said, and exploring whether quantum computing can complement supercomputers, rather than replace them, is "an important step."

That framing matters. Nobody involved is claiming Helios will solve turbine design outright. The stated goal is to test computational building blocks — the kind of subroutines that might eventually plug into a larger simulation — and see how they'd scale on Quantinuum's next machines, code-named Sol and Apollo, which don't exist yet. Riverlane CEO Steve Brierley put it as helping "accelerate the path to industrial quantum computing," language that describes a direction of travel, not a destination reached.

The work sits inside the UK's quantum strategy, which has set a target of building quantum computers capable of a trillion error-free operations — dubbed "teraQuOp" — by 2035, backed by roughly £670 million in government funding. Rolls-Royce's turbine problem is one of the test cases the UK effort wants in hand.

## Why the market shrugged

Quantinuum priced its IPO at $60 a share in early June and popped as high as $86.79 in the weeks after. By the time this deal was announced, the stock had already given back much of that gain, trading near $56 — down more than a third from its peak. The Rolls-Royce news didn't reverse the slide; shares fell further on the day, a sign investors are treating the announcement as incremental rather than a step-change.

That reaction is defensible given the numbers underneath it. Quantinuum reported first-quarter revenue of $5.24 million, down 73% year over year, against a net loss of $136.6 million. The company is still well capitalized, with $677 million in cash, and Wall Street mostly likes the stock anyway — 11 of 14 covering analysts rate it a buy, with price targets running as high as $155. But those targets are built on the promise of future revenue from deals like this one, not on cash flowing today. A signed research agreement with a marquee industrial name is good marketing and a real technical test bed; it is not a purchase order.

## What would change the calculus

The distinction that matters going forward is between validation and revenue. Partnerships like this one give quantum computing companies something to point to when asked what the technology is actually for, beyond the drug-discovery and materials-science pitches that have dominated the sector's marketing. Aerospace engineering is a genuinely hard computational problem with a customer, Rolls-Royce, that has both the budget and the incentive to find efficiency gains in engine design.

What's missing from Tuesday's announcement is anything resembling a contract value, a delivery date, or a commitment to buy quantum compute time at scale. Until Rolls-Royce is paying for capacity rather than testing algorithms, or until Quantinuum can show one of these fluid dynamics building blocks actually beating a classical supercomputer on a real design problem, this is a well-credentialed research project rather than a business. The next marker worth watching is whether either company publishes results from the Helios testing phase, or whether the collaboration quietly extends toward the paid deployment that would justify the stock's remaining premium.

totalenergies-shares-drop.headline: TotalEnergies shares slip 2.5% despite strong oil trading
totalenergies-shares-drop.body_md:
TotalEnergies shares fell as much as 2.5% in early Thursday trading, sliding to around $78.71 and underperforming rivals BP and Shell, after the French major told investors its oil-trading desk would stay strong but its liquefied natural gas business would not.

That is, on its face, an odd reason for a sub-3% move. TotalEnergies wasn't cutting its overall earnings outlook — it was raising it. Wall Street had been modeling second-quarter earnings per share of $2.75, up from $1.57 a year earlier, and the company's own trading update pointed to stronger downstream and exploration results on top of resilient oil trading. But investors zeroed in on the one line that read weaker: integrated LNG.

![Tour Total, TotalEnergies' headquarters in La Défense, Paris.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/8/89/Tour-Total.jpg)

## What actually moved

Oil trading, TotalEnergies said, is set to hold at the same strong level it reached in the first quarter, when the war between Israel and Iran disrupted crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz and pushed prices to their highest since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The company estimated the Middle East conflict is still trimming its own production by about 210,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day for the quarter — down from a 360,000 bpd hit flagged three months ago, a sign the disruption is easing rather than worsening. Downstream — refining and petrochemicals — is expected to strengthen sharply from the first quarter, and exploration and production cash flow should rise by roughly $1 billion as average liquids prices climbed $17.90 a barrel sequentially.

Set against that, integrated LNG — a division that accounts for roughly a fifth of TotalEnergies' results — is headed for a significant decline. The company said gas-trading activity underperformed after a strong first quarter, hurt by a European market that stayed flat to lower and by volatility that kept counterparties on the sidelines rather than restocking storage ahead of winter. Notably, the average price TotalEnergies realized on its own equity LNG sales actually rose, to $10.20 per million British thermal units from $9.10 a year earlier — the weakness is specifically in trading margins, not in what the company is paid for its gas.

## Reading the reaction

A move this size, on guidance this mixed, is closer to noise than signal. TotalEnergies didn't announce a writedown, a guidance cut to full-year numbers, or any structural change to its gas business — it flagged that one trading desk had a softer quarter than the last, inside a release that otherwise pointed to higher group earnings. Analysts still rate the stock a consensus Hold with an average price target near $83, comfortably above Thursday's level, and the shares trade at under 12 times earnings. Scotiabank has a price forecast as high as $97.

The distinction matters for anyone using this as a signal rather than a headline. korea-semi-selloff.headline: Korean chip stocks slide even as Taiwan Semi posts solid earnings
korea-semi-selloff.body_md:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co posted the kind of quarter chipmakers dream about Wednesday — earnings and revenue both above Wall Street's estimates, and a forecast for the current quarter that beat consensus too. The stock fell anyway. So did nearly every other chip name in Asia. The reason has less to do with Taiwan than with Seoul.

South Korea's central bank raised its benchmark interest rate a quarter point to 2.75% on Thursday, its first hike in three and a half years, after inflation ran at 3.2% in June — the hottest reading since 2023. The Bank of Korea didn't stop at one move: it signaled more increases are coming as it tries to rein in prices and prop up a weak won. Investors read that as the end of easy money for a market that had been riding a semiconductor boom to record highs, and they sold. The Kospi dropped 6.37% to 6,820.60, breaking below the 7,000 level and tripping a circuit breaker. Samsung Electronics fell 8.77%. SK Hynix, the world's dominant supplier of the high-bandwidth memory chips that feed AI data centers, dropped 11.53%. SK Square lost 12.3%; Samsung Electro-Mechanics fell 9.62%.

![A TSMC fabrication plant in Taiwan](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8a/TSMC_Fab5.JPG)

## The numbers TSMC actually posted

Strip away the sentiment and TSMC's quarter was unambiguous. The company earned $4.31 per ADR versus a $3.81 consensus, on revenue of $40.2 billion against $39.83 billion expected — a 33.7% jump from a year earlier. Gross margin hit 67.7%, and high-performance computing revenue, the bucket that includes AI accelerator chips, grew 20% from the prior quarter alone. Management didn't hedge on the outlook either: third-quarter revenue guidance of $44.6 billion to $45.8 billion cleared the $43.67 billion analysts were modeling, and TSMC lifted its full-year growth forecast from "more than 30%" to "slightly above 40%," citing AI accelerator demand and the chip-hungry compute needs of agentic AI workloads.

None of that stopped TSM shares from sliding toward technical support in early trading. When a sector-wide repricing is underway, even the company doing everything right gets pulled down with it.

## A crowded trade meets a rate shock

Part of the selloff is simple positioning math: semiconductors now account for roughly a fifth of the S&P 500's market cap, a concentration that makes any wobble in the group ripple far beyond it. Adding a Korean rate hike into that mix — raising the cost of the leverage that's financed some of the sector's run — gave momentum traders a reason to take profits, particularly in Samsung and SK Hynix after their own AI-driven rallies. The demand story underneath the two, notably for HBM memory bound for cloud AI infrastructure, hasn't broken; supply for those chips still trails demand, which is exactly why the selloff reads as a repricing of risk rather than a verdict on fundamentals.

A separate thread complicated the picture further this week. Apple won Chinese regulatory approval on July 15 to bring Apple Intelligence to iPhones sold in China, using Alibaba's Qwen model and Baidu's AI technology rather than its own. Shares of both Chinese firms jumped on the news. For chip investors it's a reminder that AI capital isn't only chasing Nvidia's and TSMC's customers — it's also flowing toward the software and model layer in China, a market that had been mostly shut out of the current AI trade.

The next test lands with Samsung's and SK Hynix's own guidance updates, and with whatever the Bank of Korea signals at its next meeting about the pace of further hikes. Until then, the gap between what TSMC's earnings say about chip demand and what Korean equities say about chip risk is likely to stay wide.

kate-spade-cmo-hire.headline: Tapestry hires L'Oréal veteran as Kate Spade's new CMO
kate-spade-cmo-hire.body_md:
Fourteen straight quarters of sales declines is the kind of streak that ends careers, and at Kate Spade New York it has. Tapestry, the handbag conglomerate that also owns Coach, has hired Allison Badea — most recently global senior vice president of brand experience at L'Oréal's Maybelline New York — as the struggling brand's new chief marketing officer. She replaces Kaisy Mae O'Reilly, who had held the job on an interim basis since early 2025.

On its own, a CMO appointment is a personnel note. This one reads as a strategy memo. Badea spent her career building prestige and mass-beauty brands inside L'Oréal's portfolio — stints at Kiehl's, Lancôme and Biotherm, plus a run as general manager of Giorgio Armani Beauty U.S. — rather than climbing up through fashion retail's discount-and-clear machinery. Tapestry did not hire a merchandising operator to plug a sales hole. It hired a brand builder.

![Kate Spade handbag](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4f/Kate_Spade_handbag.jpg)

That distinction matters because of how Kate Spade got into this hole in the first place. Quarterly sales fell roughly 10% to $219.6 million in Tapestry's most recent reporting period, down from $244.9 million a year earlier, even as the brand added 400,000 new customers — a sign that people are walking in, buying on markdown, and leaving without the brand registering. Unaided brand awareness, the metric that shows whether a name has cultural weight rather than just a coupon code, has not moved. Last August, Tapestry took an $855 million write-down tied to Kate Spade, an accounting acknowledgment that the brand was worth less than the company had been carrying it at.

## Borrowing Coach's playbook

The fix Tapestry has settled on is essentially the one that already worked next door. Coach, once similarly diluted by mall discounting, spent years pulling back wholesale distribution, cutting online flash sales and pushing prices up rather than down — a bet that scarcity sells better than clearance racks. It paid off: Coach's own quarterly sales jumped 31% to $1.7 billion, with 2.4 million new customers and, notably, real traction with Gen Z shoppers who are supposed to be allergic to legacy handbag brands.

Retail analyst Neil Saunders of GlobalData put the underlying diagnosis bluntly: Kate Spade had become "too value-oriented and overly reliant on excessive, and margin-depleting, promotions." Tapestry's plan borrows Coach's medicine — fewer flash sales, less wholesale ubiquity, higher price points — paired with a creative reset under designer Nicola Glass and a marketing push aimed squarely at younger shoppers, including more shoppable social content. Tapestry's own language for it, in a statement announcing Badea's hire, was tidier: "We're reigniting the magic of Kate Spade New York."

CEO Joanne Crevoiserat has been careful not to promise a quick turn. "What gives us confidence is that where we focus and invest, we see signs of progress," she said, adding that turnarounds take time and rarely move in a straight line. Badea's early test will be simple to state and hard to execute: can a brand known for accessible, promotion-driven fashion convince shoppers to pay more for less of it, without losing the customers who came for the discount in the first place. The next data point is Tapestry's fiscal fourth-quarter and full-year results, due in August, when analysts will be watching Kate Spade's revenue and margin lines for the first signs of whether the Coach treatment is taking.

ketamine-sellers-investigation.headline: Federal officials probe online ketamine sellers over at-home use
ketamine-sellers-investigation.body_md:
Federal regulators have opened an investigation into online retailers selling ketamine directly to consumers for use at home, according to a Wall Street Journal exclusive, part of a widening effort to rein in a drug-delivery model that grew up largely outside the traditional clinic setting.

Ketamine has lived two lives for decades: a workhorse anesthetic stocked in hospital operating rooms, and, under the street name "Special K," a party drug with a long record of abuse. What's new is the middle ground it has occupied since the pandemic — a fast-growing telehealth industry that ships vials, lozenges and nasal sprays to people's homes as an unsupervised treatment for depression and anxiety, no clinic visit required.

That business exists because of a COVID-era waiver. In 2021 the Drug Enforcement Administration relaxed its usual requirement that prescribers examine patients in person before dispensing controlled substances, a flexibility regulators have repeatedly extended and never fully unwound. It let a wave of startups build subscription-style ketamine programs on the promise of at-home relief for treatment-resistant depression — a market the Food and Drug Administration has watched swell with unapproved products it says it never signed off on.

![Ketamine, a Schedule III controlled substance, in vials seized by the Drug Enforcement Administration.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/30/Ketamine_bottles.jpg)

## A pattern of warning letters

The federal probe follows a more concrete enforcement action: on July 7, the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research sent 14 warning letters to online sellers of ketamine products, ordering nearly all of them — a dozen based in the US, one in the Netherlands — to stop marketing unapproved and misbranded drugs to American consumers. Recipients included firms trading under names like LyfeUnit, Ketamine Store and All Ketamine HCL, several pitching injectable, pharmaceutical-grade product for shipment straight to a buyer's door.[^1]

The agency's stated concern is less about ketamine's psychiatric risks than its physical ones: unregulated, potentially contaminated injectable doses, the FDA warned, can cause septicemia or sepsis in patients dosing themselves without clinical supervision.[^2] Only one ketamine-based product carries full FDA approval for psychiatric use — Johnson & Johnson's Spravato, an esketamine nasal spray cleared for treatment-resistant depression that is administered under observation, not shipped home.[^3]

## Why this is a policy story, not a market one

The companies under scrutiny are mostly private, venture-backed telehealth startups rather than publicly traded pharmaceutical firms, and the enforcement pattern so far — warning letters, not injunctions or criminal charges — has not touched Spravato's maker or any listed drugmaker's earnings. For healthcare-policy watchers, the episode is a signal that the DEA's pandemic-era telemedicine leniency is drawing renewed federal attention six years after it was first granted. For markets, it registers as background noise: a single-digit-billion-dollar niche industry, not a sector with listed exposure large enough to move index-level healthcare names.

What happens next depends on whether the DEA follows the FDA's lead. The agency has a pending rule that would tighten telemedicine prescribing of controlled substances, a proposal still unfinished as of this month; its release would be the next concrete marker of how far this scrutiny extends beyond warning letters.

[^1]: FDA, Center for Drug Evaluation and Research warning letters, issued July 7, 2026.
[^2]: FDA warning letter texts citing risk of septicemia/sepsis from unregulated injectable ketamine.
[^3]: Spravato (esketamine) FDA prescribing information, Johnson & Johnson.

floor.headline: Sound Thesis, Broken Follow-Through
floor.body_md:
The momentum-trader spotted three setups with identical technical DNA: volume spiking 17.6x the average, MACD histograms flipping positive, prices reclaiming the 20- and 50-day moving averages off a flat month. Volume-confirmed reversal, the thesis went—genuine strength, not just an RSI blown out. The market disagreed immediately.

LEDS bore the cost: 14.33% loss, wiping out the prior day's halt-driven gains. The RSI was reading 70.1 at entry, already flagging exhaustion rather than room to run—a warning the setup overrode. GSSS and SUBR each stopped at 3%. The volume spike that looked like confirmation was probably just one-session liquidation; the MACD flip lacked any follow-through buying.

Three supposedly confirmed reversals, zero persistence. The thesis itself wasn't flawed—the timing and follow-through were. Whether the bot tightens confirmation rules or accepts this as noise will shape tomorrow.
